traveler: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (Juana Ramírez de Asbaje)
title: Nepantla, the Place in the Middle: the Cell, the Four Thousand Books, and the Answer to Sor Filotea
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Nepantla, the Place in the Middle

stops.name: Nepantla, the birth between the volcanoes
stops.date_confidence: disputed: a Chimalhuacan register of 5 December 1648 supports this year, while Diego Calleja's 1700 biography gives 13 November 1651; month and day here defaulted, not asserted
stops.campa: On a hacienda between Popocatepetl and Iztaccihuatl, in a village whose Nahuatl name means the place in the middle, Isabel Ramirez bears a daughter to Pedro Manuel de Asbaje, a Basque captain who never lives under her roof. The mother cannot sign her own name. The daughter is entered as a child of the Church, the formula the parish uses for children born outside marriage. Two dates compete for this morning: 1648, from a register found at Chimalhuacan, and 1651, printed by her first biographer half a century after her death. The house keeps neither.
suggested_refs: The hacienda site at Nepantla de Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz, Tepetlixpa, State of Mexico
sources: Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Juana Ines de la Cruz', section Nacimiento
Octavio Paz, Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz o Las trampas de la fe (1982)

stops.name: Bergara, the surname that crosses the ocean
stops.date_confidence: ancestral, not a journey she makes; date carried from her birth year for placement only
stops.campa: Her father's surname comes from this town in Guipuzcoa, in the Basque provinces, and it is the only line on her family tree that reaches back across the Atlantic. Pedro Manuel de Asbaje crosses to New Spain as a captain, fathers daughters with Isabel Ramirez, marries her at no point, and leaves almost no other trace in the record. His daughter never sails to Spain. The country her name points at reaches her only as books, letters, and printed volumes carried the other way, and she will die without seeing a single street of it.
suggested_refs: Genealogical research on Pedro Manuel de Asbaje of Vergara, Guipuzcoa
sources: Octavio Paz, Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz o Las trampas de la fe (1982)

stops.name: Chimalhuacan Chalco, the register of Ines, daughter of the Church
stops.date_confidence: the register entry is dated; whether the child it names is Sor Juana is the open question
stops.campa: A priest writes into the parish book an entry for Ines, daughter of the Church, granddaughter of Pedro Ramirez and Beatriz Ramirez, with no father named. Guillermo Ramirez Espana finds the page and Alberto G. Salceda publishes it in 1952. If the child is her, she is born in 1648 and dies at forty six, which is what the convent says. If she is not, the 1651 of her biographer stands. A second entry from July 1651 names a Maria, identified as a younger sister. The font that held the water is not identified, and the coordinates mark the modern town.
suggested_refs: The Chimalhuacan baptismal register published by Alberto G. Salceda, 1952
sources: Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Juana Ines de la Cruz', section Nacimiento
Guillermo Schmidhuber, on the 1651 entry naming Maria

stops.name: Hacienda de Panoaya, the sister followed to school
stops.date_confidence: traditional, from her own retrospective account; the year follows from an assumed birth in 1648
stops.campa: At her grandfather's hacienda under the volcano, a girl of three trails her older sister to the amiga, the little school where girls are taught their letters, and tells the mistress her mother has sent her. She learns to read before anyone thinks to stop her, then keeps it quiet, expecting a beating. Pedro Ramirez keeps books and the granddaughter is given the run of them. She gives up cheese, having heard that it makes people stupid. Every line of this reaches us from her own account, written decades afterward to defend herself against a bishop.
suggested_refs: The Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz, her account of learning to read at the amiga
sources: Sor Juana, Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (1691)

stops.name: Amecameca, the parish below the pass
stops.date_confidence: regional tradition, undocumented; the year is placement only
stops.campa: The market town below the pass holds the parish that serves Panoaya, and the family walks down to it for feasts and sacraments. Local memory attaches the child's earliest formal schooling to a teacher here, briefly, before the capital takes her. No document names the classroom or the teacher. The valley keeps the story without the paper. A girl in this district who learns faster than the schooling arranged for girls has one institution above her that trains minds at all, and it is the church that will one day empty her cell of its books.
suggested_refs: The Parroquia de Nuestra Senora de la Asuncion, Amecameca

stops.name: Hacienda de Panoaya, the loa for the Blessed Sacrament
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources place the poem at age eight but date it variously to 1656 and 1658, and on Calleja's birth year it would fall in 1659
stops.campa: By eight she has written a loa for the feast of the Blessed Sacrament and won a book for it, the first payment she ever takes for verse and the only kind she wants. The prize goes onto her grandfather's shelves and comes back off again. By five she is said to be keeping the household accounts. The years of this childhood are counted differently depending on which birth date is believed, and the arithmetic never closes: on one reckoning she is eight in 1656, on the other in 1659, and the sources print both without noticing.
suggested_refs: The lost childhood loa on the Eucharist, known only by report

stops.name: Hacienda de Panoaya, the grandfather dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year in the Spanish chronology; month and day not fixed
stops.campa: Pedro Ramirez dies and the hacienda under Popocatepetl stops being a place where a granddaughter may read all afternoon. The household is broken up, the books dispersed or inherited elsewhere, and the girl is handed on to relatives. Everything she has learned so far she has taken by trespass, following a sister to school, opening a grandfather's shelves without asking. From here she will be placed rather than allowed, and every room she enters afterward has been arranged for her by somebody else.
suggested_refs: The Panoaya estate of Pedro Ramirez, Amecameca

stops.name: Yecapixtla, the years without documents
stops.date_confidence: tradition following Calleja; the years are inferred and the placement is not documented
stops.campa: Tradition puts her for a season in this Morelos town with relatives, in the gap between the hacienda and the capital. Biographers fill the years with inference because the papers are missing. The direction of travel is the only thing the record fixes: down out of the foothills of the volcanoes, toward Mexico City, out of a child's unsupervised freedom and into households and institutions that will each decide in turn what she is permitted to read. She is perhaps eight, perhaps eleven. Nobody writes it down.
suggested_refs: Diego Calleja, Vida de Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz (1700), the source of the Morelos tradition
sources: Diego Calleja, Vida de Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz (1700)

stops.name: Mexico City, the house of Maria Ramirez
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources place the move around 1656 to 1659 and the household is not identified by address
stops.campa: She is sent to the capital to live with her aunt Maria Ramirez and her uncle Juan de Mata, and stays there roughly eight years. The house is not identified and the coordinates mark the old city generally. In it she reads, and the reading is noticed. Within a few years the court will hear that a girl in a merchant household knows more theology than the men sent to test her. She arrives a hacienda child and leaves a prodigy, and the change happens in rooms nobody troubled to record the address of.
suggested_refs: The vanished household of Juan de Mata and Maria Ramirez in the colonial capital
sources: Diego Calleja, Vida de Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz (1700)

stops.name: Real y Pontificia Universidad, the door that does not open
stops.date_confidence: traditional, known only from her own retelling; the year is placement only
stops.campa: The Real y Pontificia Universidad stands facing the Plaza del Volador, and it does not admit women. She asks her mother to dress her as a boy and send her, which is the only route she can see, and her mother refuses. She never enters the building as a student. The story survives because she tells it herself, decades later, in a letter defending her right to have wanted it. The university is pulled down in 1910 and a courthouse takes the square. The refusal outlives the walls that made it necessary.
suggested_refs: The demolished Real y Pontificia Universidad de Mexico on the Plaza del Volador
sources: Sor Juana, Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (1691)
Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Real y Pontificia Universidad de Mexico'

stops.name: Mexico City, twenty lessons in Latin
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the count of twenty lessons is hers, the year is inferred from her adolescence in the capital
stops.campa: A bachiller named Martin de Olivas gives her about twenty lessons in Latin grammar. That is the whole of her formal instruction in the language she will write theology in. What she does with it is read Ovid and Virgil and the Fathers, and eventually a Portuguese Jesuit's sermon closely enough to take it apart. She counts the lessons herself when she gives an account of her education, because the number is the argument: this is what a woman does with twenty lessons and no permission to ask for more.
suggested_refs: Martin de Olivas, the bachiller who taught her Latin grammar
sources: Sor Juana, Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (1691)

stops.name: Palacio Virreinal, lady in waiting to Leonor Carreto
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day not fixed
stops.campa: At about sixteen she enters the household of Leonor Carreto, Marquesa de Mancera, wife of the viceroy, as a lady in waiting. The palace on the east side of the Zocalo is the seat of a kingdom answerable to Madrid across an ocean, and the girl from Panoaya is inside it, writing verse to order for a court that finds her wit as useful as her looks. Leonor Carreto is the first of the two vicereines who will shelter her. In the poems she is called Laura, and the friendship is not an invention of the poems.
stops.quote: I do not set store by treasures or riches; and therefore it always brings me more joy only to fix riches in my intellect and never my intellect fix on riches.
stops.quote_source: Sonnet 146, translated by Edith Grossman, in Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz: Selected Works (2014)
suggested_refs: The viceregal palace on the Zocalo, on the site of the present Palacio Nacional

stops.name: Palacio Virreinal, the forty examiners
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the whole episode rests on Calleja's posthumous Vida and no minutes or list of examiners survive
stops.campa: The viceroy, doubting the reports, assembles some forty theologians, jurists, philosophers, mathematicians, and poets and has them question her without warning before the court. She answers all of them. Diego Calleja, writing in 1700, compares her to a royal galleon fending off a swarm of small boats, and the simile is the only account there is: no minutes survive, no list of the forty, not one recorded question. The examination enters her life as a scene rather than a document, and it never leaves it again.
suggested_refs: Diego Calleja's account of the public examination, the sole source for the episode
sources: Diego Calleja, Vida de Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz (1700)

stops.name: Convento de San Jose, the Carmelite months
stops.date_confidence: attested by convent records; the colonial footprint of the house is not fixed and the coordinates are approximate
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of August she enters the Discalced Carmelites of San Jose as a postulant. The rule is built for mystics: fasting, silence, discipline, a body treated as an obstacle. Hers gives out within months and she leaves before profession, ill. She has not chosen God over marriage so much as chosen study over both, and this house leaves no hours for study. The colonial footprint of the convent is not fixed by surviving maps and the point is approximate. She will try again in two years, on better terms.
suggested_refs: The Carmelite convent of San Jose, Mexico City, her first and abandoned novitiate
sources: Diego Calleja, Vida de Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz (1700)

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, the profession
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty fourth of February she professes among the Hieronymites of Santa Paula, an order that allows a nun a private cell, personal property, servants, and visitors at the grille. She chooses it, she says afterward, as the least unsuitable arrangement available: not out of a vocation she claims to feel but out of a calculation she is willing to state aloud. She takes the name Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz. She will not pass outward through this gate again in the twenty six years she has left.
stops.quote: to have no fixed occupation which might curtail my freedom to study
stops.quote_source: Sor Juana on her reason for entering the convent, cited in Wikipedia (English) and drawn from the Respuesta a Sor Filotea
suggested_refs: The Convento de San Jeronimo, now the Universidad del Claustro de Sor Juana
sources: Sor Juana, Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (1691)

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, four thousand volumes in a cell
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the library is built up across the 1670s and 1680s and no year of completion exists
stops.campa: Inside her cell she builds what contemporaries call the largest private library in the Americas, some four thousand volumes, with mathematical and musical instruments, maps, and portraits of learned women on the walls. The figure of four thousand comes from the encyclopedists rather than from an inventory, and no shelf list survives. Visitors come to see the books nearly as often as the nun. She reads after the bell has sent the community to sleep, the one stretch of the day that belongs to nobody.
suggested_refs: The dispersed library of San Jeronimo, of which no catalogue survives
sources: Diego Calleja, Vida de Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz (1700)

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, the kitchen
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the argument is written down in the Respuesta of 1691 and the practice it describes is undated
stops.campa: Asked what a bride of Christ wants with cooking, she answers that an egg holds together in butter and oil and falls apart in syrup, that sugar passes through stages a cook can name and a philosopher cannot, and that had Aristotle cooked he would have written a great deal more. The kitchen is where she does her natural philosophy, the university being shut and the laboratory a fiction. She calls the observations trifles, then builds on them an argument that outlasts most of the theology of her century.
stops.quote: One can perfectly well philosophize while cooking supper
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sor Juana, echoing an Aragonese poet and St Teresa of Avila, per Wikipedia (English)
suggested_refs: The kitchen passage of the Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz
sources: Sor Juana, Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (1691)

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, the locutorio
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the parlor traffic runs across two decades and has no single date
stops.campa: Through the grille of the visiting parlor she receives viceroys, bishops, mathematicians, and poets who send her verses to answer and get them back sharper than they were sent. For two decades the locutorio is the nearest thing New Spain has to a salon, and it is run by a woman who cannot walk out of the room she receives in. The traffic goes one way at the door and both ways in the conversation. Every friendship she makes after 1669 is conducted through a wooden lattice, by a woman the city cannot see.
suggested_refs: The locutorio of San Jeronimo, where her correspondence and patronage were transacted
sources: Correspondence and dedications in Sor Juana's published works, 1689-1700

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, word from the Veracruz road
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year in the Spanish chronology; month and day not fixed and other accounts place the death in 1674
stops.campa: The Marquis de Mancera's term ends and the viceregal household starts for the coast. Leonor Carreto dies on the Veracruz road before reaching the ships. The nun at San Jeronimo, who cannot travel to a deathbed or a grave, hears of it by letter and answers in the only way the cloister leaves her, in verse, to a woman she had called Laura, who took a girl of sixteen out of a merchant's house and set her at the center of a court. The first of her two protectors is gone and no replacement has arrived.
suggested_refs: Sor Juana's funeral sonnets on the death of the Marquesa de Mancera

stops.name: Catedral Metropolitana, the villancicos
stops.date_confidence: attested; the villancico sets run from 1676 to 1691 and this marks the opening of the series
stops.campa: For fifteen years the cathedral chapters of Mexico and of Puebla commission her villancicos, the sung cycles performed at the great feasts, and the choirs sing words written a few streets away behind a wall. She writes Nahuatl phrases into them, and the voices of enslaved Africans and of Indians in the market, in their own cadence rather than in mockery. It is the one form of authorship the church signs a woman's name to without argument, and the tolerance lasts precisely as long as she keeps to it.
stops.quote: How clear it is they were wise, when they conceded their defeat, for it is an achievement to have bowed to the supremacy of reason!
stops.quote_source: Villancico a Catarina, translated by Kate Flores, in The Defiant Muse: Hispanic Feminist Poems (1986)
suggested_refs: The villancico sets written for the cathedrals of Mexico and Puebla, 1676-1691

stops.name: Catedral Metropolitana, the arch of Neptune
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the ceremonial entry date is not fixed here
stops.campa: For the entry of the new viceroy the cathedral chapter commissions a triumphal arch, and the program is written by a cloistered nun who cannot leave San Jeronimo to watch it raised. She casts Tomas Antonio de la Cerda as Neptune, calming the waters of a lake city built on floods, and loads the arch with a mythology no one in the procession has time to read. The text survives in print. The arch, built of wood and canvas for a single afternoon, does not. The commission puts her work in front of the incoming viceroy's wife, who will one day carry her manuscripts to Madrid.
suggested_refs: Neptuno alegorico (1680), the surviving program of a vanished arch

stops.name: Palacio Virreinal, the Condesa de Paredes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the viceroy's arrival; the friendship has no dated beginning
stops.campa: Maria Luisa Manrique de Lara, Condesa de Paredes, arrives with her husband and becomes the closest friendship of Sor Juana's life and the most consequential patron of her work. The countess comes to the locutorio, commissions poems, bears a son whose birth is celebrated with a comedy, and when she sails home she takes the manuscripts with her. Everything printed in Sor Juana's lifetime goes to press because this woman carried it across an ocean. The poems written to her are not conventionally cool.
suggested_refs: The poems to Lysi, written for Maria Luisa Manrique de Lara, Condesa de Paredes
sources: Octavio Paz, Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz o Las trampas de la fe (1982)

stops.name: Coliseo de Mexico, Los empenos de una casa
stops.date_confidence: attested by a dated performance record; the playhouse was rebuilt more than once and the coordinates are approximate
stops.campa: On the fourth of October her comedy Los empenos de una casa is staged in the capital for the celebrations around the birth of the Count of Paredes' son. It is Golden Age machinery, doors and darkness and mistaken identity, with a woman who arranges her own plot and a man dressed as a woman through the middle of it. The playwright is behind a wall a few streets off and sees none of it. Her work goes out through the city gates in a way her body never will, and comes back to her as report.
stops.quote: If you seek the love of women to win With ardor beyond compare, Why require them to be good, When 'tis you who urge their sin?
stops.quote_source: Letra de Hombres Necios Que Acusais, translated by Muriel Kittel, in The Defiant Muse: Hispanic Feminist Poems (1986)
suggested_refs: The colonial playhouse of Mexico City, demolished and rebuilt, its footprint uncertain

stops.name: Coliseo de Mexico, Amor es mas laberinto
stops.date_confidence: contested: the article on the play gives 11 January 1689, the main biographical articles give 11 February, and the two have not been reconciled
stops.campa: On the eleventh of January her second comedy is staged for the festivities around the Conde de Galve's accession to the viceroyalty. The subject is the labyrinth, Theseus and Ariadne, a thread held by a woman for a man who will leave. She writes the first and third acts and Juan de Guevara writes the second. The date is not settled: the general accounts print February, the article on the play prints January, and nobody has gone back to the record to decide. In under two years a bishop will put her theology into print without asking her.
stops.quote: In a passion that is guilty Who bears the greater blame: She who falls on being entreated Or he who falls to make entreaty?
stops.quote_source: Letra de Hombres Necios Que Acusais, translated by Muriel Kittel, in The Defiant Muse: Hispanic Feminist Poems (1986)
suggested_refs: Amor es mas laberinto, written with Juan de Guevara for the Conde de Galve's accession

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, Primero sueno
stops.date_confidence: inferred; composition is placed around 1685 and the poem is first printed in 1692
stops.campa: By candle, after the convent sleeps, she writes the poem she says is the only thing she ever composed for her own pleasure and not to order: a soul climbing through a single night toward total knowledge, failing, and waking into daylight anyway. It runs near a thousand lines through scholastic philosophy, astronomy, and the Egypt of Athanasius Kircher, whose volumes she reads and mines and whose method her circle turns into a verb. Dawn ends the ascent. The failure is the argument and she does not soften it.
stops.quote: O World, why do you wish to persecute me? How do I offend you, when I intend only to fix beauty in my intellect, and never my intellect fix on beauty?
stops.quote_source: Sonnet 146, translated by Edith Grossman, in Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz: Selected Works (2014)
suggested_refs: Primero sueno, composed around 1685 and first printed at Seville in 1692
sources: Sor Juana, Primero sueno (composed c. 1685, printed 1692)
Octavio Paz, Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz o Las trampas de la fe (1982)

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, El divino Narciso
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; the year of composition is not fixed
stops.campa: She writes an auto sacramental in which Narcissus is Christ and the pool he bends over holds human nature, and frames it with a loa in which an Aztec rite of the god of seeds is argued into a figure of the Eucharist rather than simply condemned. The characters are Occident and America, Religion and Zeal, and the conquest is staged as a debate that America is allowed to half win. It is printed in Spain and performed nowhere she can attend. The theology is orthodox. The framing is not comfortable.
suggested_refs: El divino Narciso and its loa, staging an Aztec rite as prefiguration

stops.name: Madrid, Inundacion castalida
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the imprint
stops.campa: The Condesa de Paredes, home in Spain, puts the first volume of her verse through the press of Juan Garcia Infanzon under a title calling her the Tenth Muse of Mexico. Inundacion castalida sells and is reprinted through the following decade, and a nun who has not left one building since 1669 becomes the most read poet in the Spanish language on either shore. She never crosses the ocean. Fame reaches her secondhand, in letters describing a city she will not walk and readers she will not meet.
stops.quote: You foolish men, who accuse Women without good reason, You are the cause of what you blame, Yours the guilt you deny.
stops.quote_source: Letra de Hombres Necios Que Acusais, translated by Muriel Kittel, in The Defiant Muse: Hispanic Feminist Poems (1986)
suggested_refs: Inundacion castalida, Madrid, Juan Garcia Infanzon, 1689
sources: Octavio Paz, Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz o Las trampas de la fe (1982)

stops.name: Seville, the Segundo volumen
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the first edition; the Barcelona imprint of 1693 is a reprint often miscited as the first
stops.campa: Tomas Lopez de Haro prints the Segundo volumen at Seville, and Primero sueno appears in public for the first time inside it. The Barcelona edition of the following year is a reprint, though catalogues and encyclopedias keep promoting it to first. Her books now travel a route she never takes: overland to Veracruz, across to the Andalusian ports, into the print shops, out to readers from Lima to Naples. The distance between where her name is and where her body is widens with every edition.
suggested_refs: Segundo volumen de las obras de Soror Juana Ines de la Cruz, Sevilla, Tomas Lopez de Haro, 1692

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, the critique of Vieira
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the private paper is undated and known through its printing
stops.campa: Asked in conversation what she thinks of a celebrated sermon by the Portuguese Jesuit Antonio Vieira on the greatest fineness of Christ, she takes it apart in writing, point by point, on the ground of the Fathers, with the courtesy of a woman who knows exactly how far outside her permitted territory she has walked. She writes it privately, for one reader. It is theology, and theology signed by a nun is not a genre the Holy Office keeps a shelf for. The paper leaves her cell and does not come back under her hand.
stops.quote: The sages were not ashamed to find themselves convinced; for they knew, being wise, that their knowledge was not infinite.
stops.quote_source: Villancico a Catarina, translated by Kate Flores, in The Defiant Muse: Hispanic Feminist Poems (1986)
suggested_refs: The Carta Atenagorica, her critique of Vieira's sermon on the fineness of Christ

stops.name: Puebla, the bishop prints the Carta Atenagorica
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the day is not fixed
stops.campa: Manuel Fernandez de Santa Cruz, bishop of Puebla, prints her private critique without asking, titles it Carta Atenagorica, and prefaces it with a letter of his own signed Sor Filotea de la Cruz, praising her mind and instructing her to turn it to sacred study and leave the profane alone. He is a friend doing her a favor and a bishop closing a door, both in the same gesture. She never travels to Puebla. The crisis arrives at San Jeronimo as a printed book with her name on it and a man writing in a woman's.
suggested_refs: Carta de Sor Filotea de la Cruz, Puebla, 1690
sources: Manuel Fernandez de Santa Cruz, Carta de Sor Filotea de la Cruz (Puebla, 1690)

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, the Respuesta
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated the first of March
stops.campa: On the first of March she answers. The Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz runs the length of a small book and gives her whole intellectual life as evidence: the sister followed to school, the cheese given up, the university refused, the twenty Latin lessons, the kitchen. She argues that the inclination to know is given by God and therefore cannot be a sin, that women taught women in the early church, and that ignorance is the offense. She sends it to Puebla knowing it will not help her, and sends it anyway.
stops.quote: But who has prohibited women private and individual studies? Do they not have a rational soul like men?
stops.quote_source: Autodefensa Espiritual (1690), translated from the Tapia Mendez edition (1993)
suggested_refs: La Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz, dated 1 March 1691
sources: Sor Juana, Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (1691)

stops.name: Mexico City, the flood, the riot, the famine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The lake rises, the maize fails, and the hungry riot in the capital. Preachers read the disaster as judgment on a sinful city. In a year when people are eating what they can find, a nun with four thousand books, mathematical instruments, and a reputation for arguing theology in print is an obvious thing for a church to want tidied away. Her protectors are across an ocean or dead. By the end of the next year she has stopped producing new work, and the silence is not the kind that comes of having nothing to say.
suggested_refs: The Mexico City famine and riot of 1692

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, the library sold
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day not fixed, and whether the act was voluntary is disputed in the sources themselves
stops.campa: She gives up the library. Four thousand volumes, the mathematical and musical instruments, the maps: sold or surrendered, the proceeds handed to the poor of a starving city. The sources do not agree on whether she does it freely or under compulsion, and they were never going to, since the people who could have said were the same people applying the pressure. Antonio Nunez de Miranda, her old confessor, has resumed her direction by now. The cell that visitors came to see is emptied of everything but the woman.
suggested_refs: The dispersal of the San Jeronimo library and instruments, 1694
sources: Diego Calleja, Vida de Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz (1700)

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, the signature
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the day of the vow renewal is not fixed here and the medium of the signature is contested
stops.campa: She renews her vows and signs a document of self accusation in the convent's book of professions. The manuscript survives. The tradition carried on the page itself, and repeated for three centuries since, is that she signs it in ink and in her own blood. What is not in dispute is the phrase written beneath: I, the worst of all. It circulates in two forms, la peor del mundo and la peor de todas. She has spent a life arguing that a woman may know things, and she signs the close of that argument in the first person.
stops.quote_source: Signed penitential document, Convento de San Jeronimo, 1694, quoted in Wikipedia (English); the Spanish article gives the variant 'yo, la peor del mundo'
suggested_refs: The 1694 Protesta de la fe in the Libro de Profesiones of San Jeronimo

segments.name: The Plague, and What Outlasts It

stops.name: Mexico City, the confessor dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of February her confessor dies in the city, the Jesuit who steered her into religious life as a girl and back out of her library as a woman past forty. He had dropped her direction once and taken it up again. What passed between the two of them is known mostly through men who wrote about it afterward, and each account flatters whichever of them the writer prefers. She outlives him by two months to the day, and neither leaves a version of the story the other could have answered.
stops.quote: the Mexican nun Sor Juana de la Cruz, when chastised by her confessor for her presumption in writing verse, replied that she could not help it and could not control her ability to do so; it came naturally to her and therefore must be a gift from God.
stops.quote_source: Gerda Lerner, The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993), a modern historian's reported paraphrase rather than Sor Juana's own words
suggested_refs: Antonio Nunez de Miranda, Jesuit confessor and promoter of her religious vocation
sources: Gerda Lerner, The Creation of Feminist Consciousness (1993)

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, nursing the sisters
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the epidemic and her nursing are attested, the month is not
stops.campa: An epidemic moves through the convent and the sisters begin to die. Sor Juana, with no library left to keep her at a desk, nurses them. The woman who argued that God gave her an intellect she could not decline spends her last weeks carrying water and washing bodies, the labor the order always assigned and the one no chronicler thought worth writing down until she did it. She takes the sickness from the people she is tending. The convent's records give the sequence and offer no comment on it.
suggested_refs: The 1695 epidemic in the Convento de San Jeronimo
sources: Octavio Paz, Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz o Las trampas de la fe (1982)

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, four in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She dies at about four in the morning on the seventeenth of April, aged forty six if the Chimalhuacan register is hers and forty three if her biographer is right. Twenty six years inside these walls and not one day outside them. The cell that held the largest private library in the Americas holds a dying nun and very little else. Word will take months to reach Madrid, where her books are still being reprinted, and the presses will go on selling a living author for a season after there is no author.
suggested_refs: The convent record of her death, 17 April 1695

stops.name: Convento de San Jeronimo, buried the same day
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She is buried the same day, inside the convent church, as custom requires in a plague. Carlos de Siguenza y Gongora speaks the eulogy: cosmographer, collector of Mexican antiquities, one of the few minds in the viceroyalty she could argue with as an equal and one of the few men who never asked her to stop. No marked tomb is kept. Within a century the building is altered, within two a street is cut through the block, and the exact place is lost while the name is not.
suggested_refs: Carlos de Siguenza y Gongora's funeral oration for Sor Juana

stops.name: Madrid, Fama y obras postumas
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Spanish sources give the Ruiz de Murga imprint as 1700 and the English-language accounts as 1701, unresolved
stops.campa: Ruiz de Murga prints at Madrid the third volume, Fama y obras postumas del Fenix de Mexico, gathering what survives together with a life of her by the Jesuit Diego Calleja, who never met her and wrote from letters. The sources give the imprint as 1700 and as 1701 and do not agree. Nearly everything later biography knows of her childhood comes through this book: the three year old at the amiga, the forty examiners, the galleon and the small boats. The legend and the evidence are bound in one volume.
suggested_refs: Fama y obras postumas del Fenix de Mexico, Madrid, Ruiz de Murga

stops.name: Claustro de Sor Juana, the bones and the medallion
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish source gives 1978, the English source only the 1970s; the identification of the remains has never been scientifically corroborated
stops.campa: Excavation in the block that was the Convento de San Jeronimo turns up bones and a medallion like the one she wears in her portraits, and the find is announced as hers. It has never been scientifically confirmed. The medallion passes to Margarita Lopez Portillo, sister of the president, and is handed back to Congress only in November 1995, after a deputy demands its return. The building is now the Universidad del Claustro de Sor Juana. Students cross the cloister where the library once stood.
suggested_refs: The 1978 excavation at the former Convento de San Jeronimo and the disputed remains
sources: Wikipedia (English), 'Juana Ines de la Cruz', citing New York Times coverage of the 1995 medallion return

stops.name: Palacio Legislativo de San Lazaro, the gold letters
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of the tercentennial; the day is not fixed
stops.campa: Three hundred years after her death her name is cut in gold letters into the wall of honor of the Mexican Congress, among the founders and the generals, the only one there who won nothing and commanded nobody. The country that put her on the thousand peso note, then the two hundred, then the hundred, hands her the highest civic honor it keeps for the argument it once allowed a bishop to close down. The republic canonizes what the viceroyalty required her to renounce, and does it in the same city.
suggested_refs: The muro de honor of the Mexican Congress, inscribed April 1995

stops.name: Bosque de Chapultepec, the monument and the banknote
stops.date_confidence: the 100 peso G series note is issued from 2020; the monument's installation date is not established
stops.campa: A monument stands to her in the forest of Chapultepec, another in Madrid, another before the cloister she never left alive, and her face is in every wallet in the country. Octavio Paz's biography of 1982 returns her to the center of Mexican letters, and feminist scholars retranslate the Respuesta through the decade that follows and read it as exactly what it says it is. The village where she was born carries her name now: Nepantla de Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz, the place in the middle.
suggested_refs: The Chapultepec monument, the 100 peso G series banknote, and the renamed village of Nepantla
